content.prompt: Without using a calculator, find the exact value of:

answer.worked:
The related angle for $135^{\circ}$ is $45^{\circ}$. Tangent and cosine are negative in the second quadrant.

$$\begin{align*}\sin90^{\circ}\times\tan135^{\circ}\times\cos135^{\circ}&=1\times(-\tan45^{\circ})\times(-\cos45^{\circ})\\\sin90^{\circ}\times\tan135^{\circ}\times\cos135^{\circ}&=1\times(-1)\times\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\\\sin90^{\circ}\times\tan135^{\circ}\times\cos135^{\circ}&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\end{align*}$$

The related angle for $330^{\circ}$ is $30^{\circ}$. Sine is negative in the fourth quadrant.

$$\begin{align*}\sin330^{\circ}\times\cos360^{\circ}&=-\sin30^{\circ}\times1\\\sin330^{\circ}\times\cos360^{\circ}&=-\frac12\times1\\\sin330^{\circ}\times\cos360^{\circ}&=-\frac12\end{align*}$$

$\sin360^{\circ}=0$ and $\cos330^{\circ}=\cos30^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}\sin360^{\circ}\times\cos330^{\circ}&=0\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\\sin360^{\circ}\times\cos330^{\circ}&=0\end{align*}$$

The related angle is $45^{\circ}$. In the second quadrant, sine is positive and cosine is negative.

$$\begin{align*}2\times\sin135^{\circ}\times\cos135^{\circ}&=2\times\sin45^{\circ}\times(-\cos45^{\circ})\\2\times\sin135^{\circ}\times\cos135^{\circ}&=2\times\frac1{\sqrt2}\times\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\\2\times\sin135^{\circ}\times\cos135^{\circ}&=-1\end{align*}$$

The related angle for $225^{\circ}$ is $45^{\circ}$. Sine and cosine are negative in the third quadrant. Also, $\tan180^{\circ}=0$ and $\sin90^{\circ}=1$.

$$\begin{align*}\cos225^{\circ}\times\tan180^{\circ}+\sin225^{\circ}\times\sin90^{\circ}&=\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\times0+\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\times1\\\cos225^{\circ}\times\tan180^{\circ}+\sin225^{\circ}\times\sin90^{\circ}&=0-\frac1{\sqrt2}\\\cos225^{\circ}\times\tan180^{\circ}+\sin225^{\circ}\times\sin90^{\circ}&=-\frac1{\sqrt2}\end{align*}$$

Both related angles are $60^{\circ}$. Sine is negative in the third quadrant and cosine is positive in the fourth quadrant.

$$\begin{align*}3\sin240^{\circ}-2\cos300^{\circ}&=3(-\sin60^{\circ})-2\cos60^{\circ}\\3\sin240^{\circ}-2\cos300^{\circ}&=3\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)-2\left(\frac12\right)\\3\sin240^{\circ}-2\cos300^{\circ}&=-\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}-1\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right triangle with horizontal base b, vertical right side a, hypotenuse c, theta at lower left and a right-angle square at lower right. Decorative blue edges become house black.
spec.mathematics: The opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse lengths are a, b and c; a²+b²=c². No numerical dimensions are given.

answer.worked:
$$\cos\theta=\frac bc,\qquad\sin\theta=\frac ac$$
By Pythagoras’ theorem, $a^2+b^2=c^2$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta&=\left(\frac bc\right)^2+\left(\frac ac\right)^2\\\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta&=\frac{b^2+a^2}{c^2}\\\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta&=1\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain why this result remains true when $\theta$ lies in the second quadrant.

answer.short: Cosine becomes negative, but squaring removes its sign; the same Pythagorean sum is $1$.
answer.worked:
In the second quadrant, $\cos\theta=-b/c$ and $\sin\theta=a/c$, using positive side lengths of the related-angle triangle.
$$\begin{align*}\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta&=\left(-\frac bc\right)^2+\left(\frac ac\right)^2\\\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta&=\frac{b^2+a^2}{c^2}=1\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: What happens in the other quadrants?

answer.short: The identity remains true in the third and fourth quadrants.
answer.worked: In the third quadrant both sine and cosine are negative; in the fourth only sine is negative. Squaring removes these signs, so the sum remains $(a^2+b^2)/c^2=1$.

answer.worked:
For an acute angle, $\cos\theta\ne0$. Divide the Pythagorean identity by $\cos^2\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta&=1\\\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}+\frac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}&=\frac1{\cos^2\theta}\\\left(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2+1&=\left(\frac1{\cos\theta}\right)^2\\\tan^2\theta+1&=\sec^2\theta\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Without using your calculator, find the angles $\theta$, between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ inclusive, for which:

answer.worked:
Sine is negative in quadrants III and IV. Since $\sin45^\circ=\frac1{\sqrt2}$, the related angle is $45^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\theta&=180^\circ+45^\circ\text{ or }360^\circ-45^\circ\\\theta&=225^\circ\text{ or }315^\circ\end{align*}$$

Tangent is negative in quadrants II and IV. Since $\tan30^\circ=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, the related angle is $30^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\theta&=180^\circ-30^\circ\text{ or }360^\circ-30^\circ\\\theta&=150^\circ\text{ or }330^\circ\end{align*}$$

Cosine is negative in quadrants II and III. Since $\cos30^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, the related angle is $30^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\theta&=180^\circ-30^\circ\text{ or }180^\circ+30^\circ\\\theta&=150^\circ\text{ or }210^\circ\end{align*}$$
On the unit circle, sine is the $y$-coordinate. The only point with $y=1$ is $(0,1)$, so $\theta=90^\circ$.
Cosine is the $x$-coordinate on the unit circle. The points with $x=0$ are $(0,1)$ and $(0,-1)$, so $\theta=90^\circ$ or $270^\circ$.
Since $\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, tangent is zero when $\sin\theta=0$ and $\cos\theta\ne0$. In the inclusive interval, $\theta=0^\circ,180^\circ$ or $360^\circ$.

answer.worked: The highest ordinate of the sine graph is $1$ and the lowest is $-1$. Therefore the maximum is $1$ and the minimum is $-1$.

answer.short: Maximum: $\theta=90^\circ+360^\circ k$; minimum: $\theta=270^\circ+360^\circ k$, where $k$ is any integer.

$$\begin{align*}2\sin\theta&=1\\\sin\theta&=\frac12\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}2\sin\theta&=\sqrt3\\\sin\theta&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{align*}$$
The related angle is $60^\circ$. Sine is positive in quadrants I and II.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=60^\circ\text{ or }180^\circ-60^\circ\\\theta&=60^\circ\text{ or }120^\circ\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}2\sin\theta&=-\sqrt3\\\sin\theta&=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{align*}$$
The related angle is $60^\circ$. Sine is negative in quadrants III and IV.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=180^\circ+60^\circ\text{ or }360^\circ-60^\circ\\\theta&=240^\circ\text{ or }300^\circ\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}4\cos\theta-2&=0\\4\cos\theta&=2\\\cos\theta&=\frac12\end{align*}$$
The related angle is $60^\circ$. Cosine is positive in quadrants I and IV.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=60^\circ\text{ or }360^\circ-60^\circ\\\theta&=60^\circ\text{ or }300^\circ\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}9\tan\theta&=9\\\tan\theta&=1\end{align*}$$
The related angle is $45^\circ$. Tangent is positive in quadrants I and III.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=45^\circ\text{ or }180^\circ+45^\circ\\\theta&=45^\circ\text{ or }225^\circ\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\sqrt3\tan\theta&=-1\\\tan\theta&=-\frac1{\sqrt3}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\frac1{\sqrt3}\tan\theta&=1\\\tan\theta&=\sqrt3\end{align*}$$
The related angle is $60^\circ$. Tangent is positive in quadrants I and III.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=60^\circ\text{ or }180^\circ+60^\circ\\\theta&=60^\circ\text{ or }240^\circ\end{align*}$$

The original equation requires $\cos\theta\ne0$, so $\theta\ne90^\circ,270^\circ$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta+3\cos\theta-2&=0\\(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+2)&=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$ or $\cos\theta=-2$. Reject $\cos\theta=-2$, since $-1\le\cos\theta\le1$.
The related angle is $60^\circ$. Cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants, so

answer.short:
$\theta=30^\circ,\ 150^\circ$.

Factor the quadratic and reject the root outside the range of sine.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\sin^2\theta+5\sin\theta-3&=0\\(2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta+3)&=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$ or $\sin\theta=-3$. Reject $\sin\theta=-3$, since $-1\le\sin\theta\le1$.
The related angle is $30^\circ$. Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, so
$$\theta=30^\circ,\ 180^\circ-30^\circ=150^\circ.$$

Using $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}-2(1-\sin^2\theta)+\sin\theta+1&=0\\2\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta-1&=0\\(2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta+1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$ or $\sin\theta=-1$.
For $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$, the related angle is $30^\circ$ and sine is positive in quadrants I and II, giving $\theta=30^\circ$ or $150^\circ$.
For $\sin\theta=-1$, $\theta=270^\circ$.

Since $A$, $G$ and $D$ are collinear, $\angle DGC$ is an exterior angle of triangle $AGC$.

entries.description:
In Chapter 12, we saw how to extend the definition of the trigonometric functions to the second quadrant so that we could deal with obtuse-angled triangles. You probably realised that the ideas could be further extended so that we could give meaning to the trigonometric ratios of angles that were greater than 180°. We will do that in this chapter, and we will also draw the graphs of the trigonometric functions for all positive and negative angle sizes.

The graphs of sine and cosine functions are used to model wave motion and are therefore central to the applications of mathematics to any problem in which periodic motion is involved – from the motion of the tides and ocean waves to sound waves and modern telecommunications.

We take a circle of radius 1, centre the origin, in the Cartesian plane.
From point P on the circle in the first quadrant, we construct the right-angled triangle POQ with O at the origin. Let ∠POQ be θ.
The length OQ is the x-coordinate of P, and since OQ/1 = cos θ, the x-coordinate of P is cos θ.
Similarly, the y-coordinate of P is the length PQ, which equals sin θ.
Hence, the coordinates of the point P are (cos θ, sin θ).

entries.description:
Since the sine and cosine of an angle are the y- and x-coordinates of the corresponding point P, sin (θ + 360°) = sin θ, cos (θ + 360°) = cos θ, sin (θ − 360°) = sin θ and cos (θ − 360°) = cos θ.
It is clear that for any angle greater than 360° or less than 0°, the corresponding point P on the unit circle can be equivalently described by an angle between 0° and 360°.
Hence, to find the trigonometric function of an angle greater than 360°, we subtract a multiple of 360° to arrive at an angle between 0° and 360°.
Similarly, to find the trigonometric function of a negative angle, we add a multiple of 360° to arrive at an angle between 0° and 360°.

entries.description:
We will examine the symmetries of the graph of y = cos θ in the exercises.
The values of cos θ remain the same when θ is increased or decreased by 360°; that is, cos θ = cos (θ + 360°). cos θ is periodic with period 360°.

Note that the graph of cosine is symmetric about the y-axis.
You should also notice that the graph of y = cos θ is the same as the graph of y = sin θ translated to the left by 90°. That is, cos θ = sin (90° + θ).
